newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Aussie, Canadian bonds keep appeal.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Aussie, Canadian bonds keep appeal.

text.p: Australian and Canadian bonds retain their appeal for investors seeking outperformance of U.S. Treasuries, but there is cause for wariness, analysts said.

"Canada probably offers the best prospects (among dollar bloc markets) over the next few weeks," said Michael Derks at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "Australia looks better than New Zealand, but not by a great deal."
Canadian bonds topped Salomon Brothers' World Government Bond index with 1.34 percent returns in local currency terms for the week ended on Thursday.
Derks, an international fixed income strategist, suggested investors should concentrate on the long end of the Canadian bond yield curve, but the short end in the other two markets.
Dick Howard, senior economist at Julius Baer Investments, said he favoured the dollar bloc in general over European bonds and certainly Japanese debt.
But he felt the Bank of Canada had already cut interest rates slightly too far, even before Friday's quarter-point cut to 3.25 percent in bank rate.
"Our strategy is to be overweight Australian bonds but hedge into either U.S. or Canadian dollars," Howard said, adding that Australia's economic fundamentals were more attractive.
The Australian 10-year bond yield spread over Treasuries, now at 100 basis points, could narrow to 50 by the end of this year or even sooner, he said.
Kevin Atwill, senior dealer at Commonwealth Bank, said he expected the Australian yield spread to be down to 75 basis points by the end of 1996 with 50 a longer term target .

"We have seen a lot of money going back into Australia from New Zealand bonds in the last three or four weeks as people take profits and the political situation in New Zealand has become unclear," Atwill said.
There was also a risk markets would lose patience with Kiwi bonds if negotiations to form a coalition government after inconclusive elections dragged on much longer.

Atwill said the short end of the Aussie market had already started to discount the next interest rate cut after Wednesday's 1/2 point rate cut to 6.50 percent, although the next cut was probably months away and would depend on economic data.
According to Derks, dollar bloc markets might face more difficult conditions in the next few months if Japan changed its yen policy and sent interest rates moving upwards.
"I have been pretty positive on peripheral dollar markets for the last few months but now I am more cautious," he said.
Howard said the Australian economy may turn out to be a little weaker and inflation more subdued than the market now believed -- both factors which would boost Aussie bonds.

But any increase in Japanese interest rates could hurt this favourable outlook, he said, referring to comments on Thursday by Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara that the dollar's correction from last year's sharp slide against the yen was about to end.
Any rise in Japanese rates could entice Japanese funds back home from their present heavy investment in the short end of the Australian yield curve, Howard said.

On New Zealand, Howard said he liked the bonds but was suspicious of the currency. While the central bank might cut interest rates by the end of the year, it was unikely to do so before the shape of the new government and its fiscal policy became clearer," he said.
Derks said a New Zealand rate cut by Christmas was more than likely and a subsequent cut was probable in the first three or four months of 1997.
